And Goethe, who was particularly sensitive to the rich
and many-hued beauties of the world, knows nevertheless
that two souls dwell in our breast and so prays:
"Thou visitant from heaven, who dost soothe all pain and
sorrow, and on him whose misery passes measure dost heap
a twofold blessing: Ah! weary am I of earth's troubles!
What meaneth pain and sorrow? Sweet peace, come gently
down and steal into my breast!"
But the New Testament speaks otherwise than the poets
about man's strangeness and homelessness in the world. It
does not sound the note of longing, born of weariness and
disillusionment or of surfeit, for there the challenge to the
world is sounded as a result of the intervention of God's
power. This challenge is not to be understood in the sense
that the Christian faith intrudes to set the world and its
problems to rights. But on the other hand it would also be a
misunderstanding to suppose that the Christian gospel called
men out of the world, so that they no longer had any share
in either its gifts or its tasks. It is a question of one thing only:
to say to the world that it is not the final power which can
claim dominion over men.
Just as the hostility of the world was directed to the
mission of Jesus who summoned men to surrender themselves
to the sovereignty of God (for "no man can serve two
masters") and to seek first His kingdom, so it is likewise
aroused by the preaching of His Church. Nor does it need
to be a formal preaching expressed in audible words. The
very existence in the world of the Christian Church is a
protest against the world; a protest against the presumption
of the world to be able to impose ultimate duties and
obligations, to give lasting satisfaction and fulfilment. A
protest too against the world's claim to be holy: for one alone
is holy, namely, God, the Lord of the world. For such reasons
the world feels the Church to be an alien body in its midst,
and if the Church refuses to yield to the sway of the world
